title: Why the rating stops
caption_hook: Is your child's rating stuck? It's rarely talent 👇
caption_body: Most plateaus come from training without structure, not from a lack of talent.

scenes.headline: Stuck in chess?
scenes.narration: Watching your talented child stay stuck at the same rating, month after month, is hard.

scenes.headline: More games won't fix it
scenes.narration: Random videos and endless blitz feel like practice. But without a plan, kids repeat the same mistakes.

scenes.headline: Kids need a roadmap
scenes.narration: Strong players follow a roadmap, one skill at a time, in the right order for their level.

scenes.headline: Train with International Masters
scenes.narration: That's how our students train, with International Masters, in small groups of kids at their level.

scenes.headline: Structure beats talent
scenes.narration: With structure and feedback, progress stops being luck and becomes a plan.

title: The blitz trap
caption_hook: Hours of blitz, same rating? Here's why ⚡
caption_body: Fast games are fun, but they rarely teach new skills on their own.

scenes.headline: Hours of blitz, no progress?
scenes.narration: Your child plays blitz for hours, and the rating barely moves. Sometimes it even drops.

scenes.headline: Fast games, same mistakes
scenes.narration: In fast games there's no time to think, and nobody reviews the mistakes afterwards.

scenes.headline: A coach sees the pattern
scenes.narration: In Square 65, Key forty-four is about kids who move too fast. A coach finds that pattern and fixes it.

scenes.headline: What works instead
scenes.narration: Slower games, a review of every loss, and exercises aimed at that exact weakness.

scenes.headline: Then results come
scenes.narration: That's when the rating starts climbing again, and the confidence comes back with it.

title: Groups or private?
caption_hook: Group or private chess lessons? The honest answer 👇
caption_body: Both work. It depends on your child's level, goals and personality.

scenes.headline: Groups or private?
scenes.narration: Parents ask us this all the time. Should my child train in a group, or with a private coach?

scenes.headline: Why small groups work
scenes.narration: Small groups of kids at the same level give real sparring partners and a healthy push.

scenes.headline: When private is better
scenes.narration: Private lessons are best for advanced players working on their own openings and mistakes.

scenes.headline: We offer both
scenes.narration: That's why we offer both, always with International Masters, and we help you choose.

title: How much time per week?
caption_hook: How many hours of chess a week does a child need? ⏱️

scenes.headline: How much practice?

params.question: How many hours a week should my child train?

scenes.narration: How much should a child practice chess every week? It's less about hours than you think.

scenes.headline: Consistency wins
scenes.narration: Short daily exercises, regular lessons, and slow games beat one long weekend session.

scenes.headline: The right order matters
scenes.narration: And the order matters. Each skill builds on the last one, like steps on a roadmap.

scenes.headline: Built into every week
scenes.narration: That's why our students get weekly assignments, recorded lessons and regular progress reports.

title: The roadmap by level
caption_hook: What should your child learn next in chess? 🗺️
caption_body: Every level needs different skills. Training the wrong ones wastes months.

scenes.headline: Training the wrong things?
scenes.narration: Many kids study hard, but they study things that don't match their level yet.

scenes.headline: Six levels, one roadmap
scenes.narration: Our roadmap has six levels, from the basics all the way to master level.

scenes.headline: What changes at each level
scenes.narration: First tactics and checkmates, then calculation and endgames, then plans and a real opening repertoire.

scenes.headline: Guided by International Masters
scenes.narration: Our coaches place each child on the right step, and move them up when they're ready.

scenes.headline: Steady, measurable progress
scenes.narration: That's how progress becomes steady and measurable, instead of random.

title: The power of game review
caption_hook: The habit that separates improving kids from stuck ones 🔍
caption_body: Every lost game is a free lesson, if someone helps your child read it.

scenes.headline: Losses hurt
scenes.narration: Losing a tournament game hurts. Most kids just want to forget it and play the next one.

scenes.headline: Every loss is a lesson
scenes.narration: But every loss shows exactly what to train next, if someone helps them read it.

scenes.headline: How we review games
scenes.narration: We find the turning point, name the pattern behind it, and train that pattern until it's gone.

scenes.headline: With real masters
scenes.narration: Our students review their games with International Masters, and keep every lesson recorded.

scenes.headline: Fewer mistakes, more wins
scenes.narration: Fewer repeated mistakes means more wins, and a lot more confidence at the board.

title: From 1100 to 1800+
caption_body: A real story from our academy. Structure plus the right coach, month after month.

scenes.headline: It started at 1100
scenes.narration: One of our students started at eleven hundred, like many kids who love chess but feel stuck.

scenes.headline: 13 months later
scenes.narration: With a clear roadmap and regular coaching, the rating climbed past eighteen hundred in thirteen months.

scenes.headline: And kept going
scenes.narration: And it didn't stop there. The same student later crossed twenty three hundred FIDE and became a National Master.

scenes.headline: Not luck. Method.
scenes.narration: It wasn't luck. It was the right method, the right coaches, and consistent work.

title: A champion's path
caption_hook: State Champion at 10. International Master at 14 🏆
caption_body: A real path from one of our students, step by step.

scenes.headline: Every champion starts small
scenes.narration: Every champion starts as a kid who loves the game and wants to get better.

scenes.headline: A champion's path
scenes.narration: One of our students became State Champion at ten, National Master at twelve, and International Master at fourteen.

scenes.headline: What made the difference
scenes.narration: A clear roadmap, serious tournament preparation, and expert coaching at every step.

scenes.headline: Talent needs a plan
scenes.narration: Talent matters. But talent with a plan is what turns a promising kid into a champion.

title: Videos are not training
caption_hook: Hours of chess videos, same rating? Key 3 explains why 📘
caption_body: From Square 65 by IM Alberto Chueca: replace passive watching with deliberate practice.

scenes.headline: Watching isn't training
scenes.narration: Your child watches chess videos for hours. It feels like study, but the rating doesn't move.
In Square 65, IM Alberto Chueca puts it simply. Watching videos is entertainment, not training.

scenes.headline: Deliberate practice
scenes.narration: Solve without moving the pieces, write down your variations, then compare. No effort, no progress.

scenes.headline: One concept at a time
scenes.narration: That's how our students train. One study thesis at a time, guided by International Masters.

title: Inside a 90-minute class
caption_hook: What happens inside a high-performance chess class? 🧠
caption_body: The T-T-P system from Square 65: tactics, theory, practice. Every class, every level.

scenes.headline: What happens in class?

params.question: What happens inside a high-performance chess class?

scenes.narration: Parents often ask us what actually happens in a ninety-minute class. Here's our system.
It's Key six of Square 65. The Tripartite Training System, what we call T-T-P.

scenes.headline: Three phases, every class
scenes.narration: First a tactics warm-up. Then one strategic recipe. Then games that force the new concept to appear.

scenes.headline: Concepts that stick
scenes.narration: Class after class, each concept becomes a weapon your child actually uses in tournaments.
